title: The Mary Celeste (2)
subtitle: Atlantic Ocean, 1872
vo: December eighteen seventy-two. A sailing ship was found drifting in the Atlantic with no one aboard. She was still seaworthy. Her cargo, seventeen hundred barrels of alcohol, was almost untouched. There was plenty of food and water. Ten people had sailed on her: the captain, his wife, their two-year-old daughter and seven crew. The ship's only boat was gone. Her last log entry, nine days earlier, put her off the Azores, nearly four hundred nautical miles from where she was found. No one has ever proved why they left. Not one of the ten was ever seen again.

title: The Double Flash
subtitle: The Vela Incident · Indian Ocean, 1979
vo: In September nineteen seventy-nine, an American satellite detected a double flash of light, over the southern Indian Ocean. A double flash is the signature of a nuclear weapon. The brief, intense initial flash. The second, expanding fireball. It was never officially explained. Forty years of scholarship lean toward a joint test, by two governments that have never confirmed it. The United States has never reclassified the event. The file remains, officially, ambiguous.

title: The Voynich Manuscript
subtitle: Italy, 1912
vo: In nineteen twelve, a rare book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a manuscript that no one could read. About two hundred and forty pages, handwritten, in a script no one has ever identified. Page after page of plants. Almost none can be clearly identified. In two thousand nine, carbon dating placed its parchment in the early fourteen hundreds. Codebreakers, linguists, and computers have all tried. It has never been convincingly deciphered.
first: In nineteen twelve, a rare book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a manuscript that no one could read.
caption:
In 1912, the rare book dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought a manuscript in Italy that no one could read: about 240 handwritten pages in an unidentified script, filled with drawings of plants that almost no one can clearly identify. In 2009, radiocarbon dating at the University of Arizona placed its parchment between 1404 and 1438. It is now held at Yale's Beinecke Library. Codebreakers, linguists and computers have all tried; no decipherment has ever been verified.

Still unsolved.

title: The Flannan Isles Keepers
subtitle: Eilean Mòr · Outer Hebrides, 1900
vo: Eilean Mòr, in the Outer Hebrides. December, nineteen hundred. A passing ship saw that the island's lighthouse was dark. Weather held off the relief boat until Boxing Day. When it landed, the three keepers were gone. The lamps were cleaned and ready. The clock had stopped. One set of oilskins was still inside. At the west landing, iron railings were twisted, and a block of stone weighing over a ton had been moved. The inquiry believed a great wave had swept them away. No trace of the three men was ever found.

title: The Waratah
subtitle: SS Waratah · off South Africa, 1909
vo: South Africa, July nineteen-oh-nine. The Waratah, a big new liner, left Durban for Cape Town. She never arrived. Two hundred and eleven people were aboard. None was ever seen again. Early the next morning, another steamer exchanged lamp signals with her. It was the last confirmed sighting. One passenger left the ship at Durban. He later cabled his wife that he had thought her top-heavy. For decades, searchers combed that coast. One promising wreck turned out to be another ship. The Waratah has never been found.

title: Food on the Table
subtitle: The Mary Celeste · Atlantic Ocean, 1872
vo: In December 1872, a ship was found adrift in the Atlantic, between the Azores and Portugal. The Mary Celeste was in good order. Her cargo was untouched. There was food on the table. The captain, his wife, their daughter, and seven crew were all gone. A single lifeboat was missing. No sign of storm. No sign of violence. No sign of anyone. What happened on that ship has never been determined.

title: The Search for the Waratah
subtitle: SS Waratah · off South Africa, 1909 · the search, 1999–2004
vo: South Africa, nineteen ninety-nine. Searchers announced they had found the Waratah, the liner lost ninety years before. She had left Durban in nineteen-oh-nine with two hundred and eleven aboard. None was ever seen again. Explorer Emlyn Brown's sonar had found a wreck off that coast whose outline seemed to match. Two years later, a dive reached it. It was another ship: a wartime freighter, lost in nineteen forty-three. In two thousand four, after more than twenty years, he said he had no idea where else to look. The Waratah has never been found.
first: South Africa, nineteen ninety-nine. Searchers announced they had found the Waratah, the liner lost ninety years before.
caption:

Two years later, a dive showed it was another ship, the Nailsea Meadow, a wartime freighter lost in 1943. In 2004, after more than twenty years, Brown said he had exhausted his options and no longer knew where to look. The Waratah has never been found.

title: Star Tiger
subtitle: Star Tiger · North Atlantic, 1948
vo: The Atlantic, January nineteen forty-eight. A British airliner, the Star Tiger, was flying through the night to Bermuda. It never arrived. Just after three in the morning, she asked Bermuda for a radio bearing. Nothing more was heard. Thirty-one people were aboard. The search found no wreckage. No one aboard was ever seen again. The official inquiry wrote that no more baffling problem had ever been presented for investigation. Theories include fuel running out, and sabotage. The wreck has never been found.

title: The Voynich Manuscript: the vellum test
subtitle: Tucson, 2009 · Beinecke MS 408
vo: Tucson, two thousand nine. A lab tests four slivers of vellum from a book that has never been deciphered. One theory said the dealer who bought it in nineteen twelve, Wilfrid Voynich, had faked it himself. The slivers came from four different pages. All four dated the skin to the early fourteen hundreds. That dates the skin, not the writing. But nothing in the inks or paints was out of place for that time. A modern fake now looks unlikely. Yet no one has proved what a single word of it says.
first: Tucson, two thousand nine. A lab tests four slivers of vellum from a book that has never been deciphered.
caption:
In 2009, a radiocarbon lab at the University of Arizona in Tucson tested four slivers of vellum from the Voynich manuscript, a book that has never been deciphered. One theory held that Wilfrid Voynich, the book dealer who bought it in 1912, had faked it himself. The four samples came from four different pages, and all four dated the skin to the early 1400s, roughly 1404 to 1438. That dates the skin, not the writing, and the ink itself was not dated. But nothing in the inks or paints was out of place for that time. A modern fake now looks unlikely. Yet no one has proved what a single word of it says.

Still unsolved.

title: The Other Clues
subtitle: The Vela Incident · 1979–1980
vo: September nineteen seventy-nine. A satellite saw a double flash over the Indian Ocean. Hours later in Puerto Rico, the Arecibo radio telescope recorded a ripple high in the atmosphere. Moving in an unusual direction. Underwater microphones caught sounds a Navy laboratory linked to a blast at sea. Weeks later, sheep in Australia were found carrying iodine one thirty-one, a product of nuclear fission. In nineteen eighty, a panel for the White House judged it probably not nuclear. Many government scientists disagreed. None of it settled the question. No government has ever confirmed what it was.
first: September nineteen seventy-nine. A satellite saw a double flash over the Indian Ocean. Hours later in Puerto Rico, the Arecibo radio telescope recorded a ripple high in the atmosphere.
caption:
September 1979. An American satellite recorded a double flash over the southern Indian Ocean. Hours later, the Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico picked up a ripple in the upper atmosphere, moving in an unusual direction. In October and November, iodine-131, a product of nuclear fission, turned up in the thyroids of sheep in southeastern Australia. In 1980, a panel convened for the White House judged the flash probably not a nuclear explosion. Many government scientists disagreed. No government has ever confirmed what it was.

title: The Flannan Isles Light (2)
subtitle: Outer Hebrides, 1900
vo: Scotland, December nineteen hundred. On a remote island in the Atlantic, the lighthouse went dark. Storms held the relief boat back until Boxing Day. High on the west cliff, a box of ropes kept a hundred and ten feet above the sea had been smashed open. The inquiry blamed an unusually large wave. Not one of the three keepers was ever found.

title: The Voynich Manuscript (2)
subtitle: Yale · Beinecke MS 408
vo: Yale University keeps a book, six hundred years old, that no one has ever been able to read. It is written in an alphabet of its own. Twenty or so letters, page after page, that no one has matched to any known language. It is full of drawings: plants nobody can name, circles like star charts, and pools of water linked by pipes. The calfskin it is written on has been carbon dated to the early fourteen hundreds. Wartime codebreakers tried. So have linguists, and computers. No reading has ever been proved.

caption:

Its drawings show plants nobody can name, circular charts like star maps, and pools of water linked by pipes. Wartime codebreakers, linguists and computers have all tried. title: Rongorongo
subtitle: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) · 1864
vo: Rapa Nui, Easter Island. In eighteen sixty-four, a missionary wrote of carved wooden tablets in almost every house. Rows of tiny figures. Each line runs the other way, and the tablet is turned to read it. In the eighteen-sixties, slave raids and disease devastated the island. Many who knew the script were lost. About two dozen carved objects survive. In twenty twenty-four, the wood of one was dated to the fourteen hundreds. One passage may be a lunar calendar. No reading of the script has ever been accepted.
first: Rapa Nui, Easter Island. In eighteen sixty-four, a missionary wrote of carved wooden tablets in almost every house.
caption:
1864, Rapa Nui (Easter Island). A missionary wrote that wooden tablets carved with rows of tiny signs were kept in almost every house. The lines alternate direction; the reader turns the tablet around at the end of each one. In the 1860s, slave raids and disease devastated the island, and many who knew the script were taken or died. About two dozen inscribed wooden objects survive, in museums around the world. In 2024, the wood of one tablet held in Rome was radiocarbon-dated to around 1500, long before the first European ships arrived in 1722. Part of one text may record a lunar calendar. No proposed reading of the script has ever been accepted.

Still unsolved.

title: All Sails Set
subtitle: The Carroll A. Deering · Cape Hatteras, 1921
vo: Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. January thirty-first, nineteen twenty-one. A five-masted schooner sits aground on Diamond Shoals, all sails set. The Carroll A. Deering. Her two lifeboats were gone. So were the ship's log, the navigation equipment, and the crew's belongings. In the galley, food had been laid out for a meal. Rescuers found a cat aboard. Of the eleven men, there was no sign. Five federal departments investigated. Piracy, mutiny, rum-runners, a hurricane. Each was a theory. None was proven. The crew was never found.

title: The Dorabella Cipher
subtitle: Elgar's note to Dora Penny · England, 1897
vo: England, July eighteen ninety-seven. The composer Edward Elgar slipped a short note into his wife's letter to a young friend, Dora Penny. It held no words. Just eighty-seven small curved marks, in three lines, turned in different directions. Dora could make nothing of it. She put it away, and kept it for about forty years. In nineteen thirty-seven, she printed a copy in her memoir. The original has since been lost. Many have claimed to break it. In two thousand seven, the Elgar Society held a competition. No solution has ever been generally accepted.
first: England, July eighteen ninety-seven. The composer Edward Elgar slipped a short note into his wife's letter to a young friend, Dora Penny.
caption:

The original is now thought lost. Many have claimed to break it, and no solution has ever been generally accepted.

title: Croatoan
subtitle: The Roanoke Colony · North Carolina, 1587–1590
vo: In fifteen eighty-seven, more than a hundred English settlers landed on Roanoke Island, off the coast of North Carolina. Their governor sailed for England for supplies. War delayed him for three years. When he returned, in fifteen ninety, the colony was abandoned. The houses had been dismantled. There were no bodies. There was no sign of attack. Carved into a palisade post, one word: Croatoan. Carved into a tree, the letters: C-R-O. The settlers were never found. The colony is now four hundred years old, and still unanswered.

title: The Rongorongo Wood
subtitle: Rome · 2024 (Rapa Nui)
vo: Twenty twenty-four. The wood of an Easter Island tablet kept in Rome was dated. The tree was cut down around fifteen hundred. Two centuries before Europeans arrived. If the writing is that old, islanders may have invented it alone. Only a handful of places ever have. But dating the wood is not dating the carving. The authors say so themselves. And this wood never grew on the island. It may have drifted ashore, or come off a European ship. Fewer than thirty carved objects survive. The script has never been deciphered.
first: Twenty twenty-four. The wood of an Easter Island tablet kept in Rome was dated. The tree was cut down around fifteen hundred.
caption:
2024. Scientists radiocarbon-dated four rongorongo tablets from Rapa Nui (Easter Island), kept in Rome. The wood of one, a notched tablet called Échancrée, came from a tree felled around 1500, more than two centuries before Europeans arrived in 1722. If the writing is that old, the islanders may have invented it on their own, as only a handful of places in history ever have. But dating the wood is not dating the carving, and the study's authors say so. That wood never grew on the island; it may have drifted ashore or come off a European ship. Some linguists question whether the script is full writing at all. Fewer than 30 inscribed objects survive, and the script has never been deciphered.

Still unsolved.

title: The Mary Celeste and Conan Doyle
subtitle: Atlantic Ocean, 1872 · Cornhill Magazine, 1884
vo: The Atlantic, eighteen seventy-two. The Mary Celeste was found drifting, empty. But the Marie Celeste most people know comes from a young Arthur Conan Doyle. In eighteen eighty-four, before Sherlock Holmes, his story ran unsigned, told as a survivor's statement. In it, her boats were still aboard. Even the American consul at Gibraltar asked if it was true. In fact, her only boat was gone. Her cargo was nearly untouched. There was food and water for six months. The story was invented. The empty ship was real. The ten aboard were never found.

caption:

In fact her only boat was gone, her cargo of alcohol was nearly untouched, and she carried food and water for six months. The story was invented. The empty ship was real. The ten people aboard were never found.

title: The Patch
subtitle: John White's map · British Museum, 2012
vo: The British Museum, twenty twelve. Researchers lit a four-hundred-year-old map from beneath. John White drew it. Under a small paper patch was a hidden fort, drawn in bright red and blue. White governed the Roanoke colony. In fifteen ninety, he found it deserted, with one word carved on a post: Croatoan. He wrote that the settlers had planned to move fifty miles inland. The fort lies where two rivers meet. Digs near the spot have found English pottery. Why the fort was covered is unknown. Where the colonists went has never been proved.
first: The British Museum, twenty twelve. Researchers lit a four-hundred-year-old map from beneath. John White drew it.
caption:

He wrote that the settlers had planned to move fifty miles inland. Digs near that spot have found a few English pottery sherds. Why the symbol was covered is unknown, and where the colonists went has never been proved.

title: The Loneliest Whale
subtitle: The 52-hertz whale · North Pacific, 1989
vo: The North Pacific, nineteen eighty-nine. Navy hydrophones, built to hear submarines, picked up a whale call at fifty-two hertz. Too high for a blue whale. Too high for a fin whale. Woods Hole scientists tracked it for twelve years, from nineteen ninety-two to two thousand four. It matched no known species. The press called it the loneliest whale in the world. Theories include a hybrid, or an unusual body. The singer has never been identified.

title: The Taos Hum
subtitle: Taos · New Mexico, 1993
vo: By nineteen ninety-three, so many people in Taos, New Mexico, had complained about a sound that their members of Congress asked for an investigation. A low hum. A rumble. A drone. Only about two in every hundred people said they could hear it. That summer, scientists from Sandia, Los Alamos, the Air Force and the University of New Mexico brought instruments to Taos to measure it. Hearers matched its pitch: very low, between thirty and eighty hertz. The instruments never found the source. Hums like it have been reported around the world. Most have never been traced.

title: The Cyclops
subtitle: USS Cyclops · Atlantic Ocean, 1918
vo: March, nineteen eighteen. The Navy coal ship Cyclops left Barbados for Baltimore with about three hundred people aboard. She was never seen again. No distress call was ever received. No wreckage was ever found. In her hold, about ten thousand tons of manganese ore, bound for wartime munitions. Theories include a storm, a broken hull, or a German submarine. None has been proven. Often told as a Bermuda Triangle story, she remains one of the largest non-combat losses in US Navy history. Her wreck has never been found.

title: The Jamison Family
subtitle: Latimer County · Oklahoma, 2009
vo: In October two thousand nine, Bobby and Sherilynn Jamison and their six-year-old daughter, Madyson, drove into the hills of southeastern Oklahoma to look at land. title: The Joyita
subtitle: South Pacific · 1955
vo: South Pacific, November nineteen fifty-five. A small ship was found drifting north of Fiji. Everyone aboard was gone. The Joyita had left Samoa five weeks earlier, on a two-day run to Tokelau, with twenty-five people aboard. She was found more than six hundred miles off course, partly submerged, kept afloat by the cork lining her hull. Her radio was tuned to the distress frequency. The clocks had stopped at ten twenty-five. The life rafts were gone. No one aboard was ever found. The inquiry called their fate inexplicable on the evidence.

title: The Witness

title: The Indus Script
subtitle: Indus Valley · c. 2600–1900 BCE
vo: The Indus Valley, more than four thousand years ago. People carved small stone seals, most with an animal, and a short row of signs. No one has ever deciphered them. Some scholars have argued the signs may not be writing at all. More than a hundred decipherments have been proposed. None has been accepted.

title: Linear A

vo: Crete, around nineteen hundred. Arthur Evans's excavations found clay tablets in a script he named Linear A. Today we can sound it out. We still cannot read it. None has been accepted.

title: Upsweep

A long train of rising tones, each several seconds long, loud enough to be recorded across the Pacific. It became known as Upsweep, and in the recordings it seems seasonal, peaking in spring and autumn. Its source lies roughly in the remote South Pacific, between New Zealand and South America. Whales were an early guess, but the tone barely varies. It lies near what may be undersea volcanic activity, and it has grown fainter since 1991. NOAA still calls its origin unresolved.

Still unsolved.

title: The Devil's Footprints
subtitle: The Devil's Footprints · Devon, 1855
vo: Devon, England, February eighteen fifty-five. After heavy snow, people woke to lines of small hoof-shaped prints. Mostly in single file, about four inches long. Reports said they crossed rooftops and high walls. They were reported in more than thirty places, on both sides of the Exe estuary. Some said the Devil had walked. One letter at the time claimed a trail ran a hundred miles in a night. The farthest anyone is known to have followed one was about five. Donkeys, wood mice, a runaway balloon, a hoax. All remain theories. None explains every mark.
first: Devon, England, February eighteen fifty-five. After heavy snow, people woke to lines of small hoof-shaped prints.
caption:
February 1855, south Devon, England. After a night of heavy snow, people woke to find lines of small hoof-shaped prints, about four inches long, mostly in single file. They were reported in more than 30 places, on both sides of the Exe estuary, and reports said they crossed rooftops and high walls. Some said the Devil had walked, and it was spoken of from the pulpit. One letter at the time claimed a trail ran over a hundred miles in a single night; the farthest anyone is known to have followed one was about five miles. Donkeys, wood mice, a runaway balloon and a hoax have all been suggested. None has ever explained every mark.

title: HMS Atalanta
subtitle: Bermuda, 1880
vo: Bermuda, January eighteen eighty. The training ship Atalanta sailed for England, with about two hundred and eighty aboard. Most were young trainees. The ship never arrived. None of them was ever seen again. Wreckage was reported near the Azores. None of it was ever proven to be hers. A former crewman said she rolled dangerously. No trace of her was ever found. Theories include a storm, and a ship too unstable to sail. More than a century on, no wreck has ever been identified.

caption:

None of them was ever seen again. Wreckage was reported near the Azores, but none of it was ever proven to be hers. A former crewman said she rolled dangerously; no trace of her was ever found. title: The D'Agapeyeff Cipher
subtitle: The challenge in Codes and Ciphers · London, 1939
vo: London, nineteen thirty-nine. The cryptographer Alexander d'Agapeyeff published a book called Codes and Ciphers. At the end, he printed a challenge. Rows of numbers, in groups of five. He later reportedly admitted that he no longer knew how he had enciphered it. The challenge was left out of later editions. Codebreakers have studied it ever since. First by hand, then by computer. Some think he made a mistake when he enciphered it. No solution has ever been generally accepted.

title: The Billboard on the Highway
subtitle: The Sodder Children · West Virginia, 1945
vo: On Christmas night, nineteen forty-five, a fire destroyed the Sodder family home in the West Virginia hills. Five of the ten Sodder children were never seen again. No bones were found in the ashes. A coroner issued death certificates without remains. Twenty-two years later, a photograph arrived in the mail. The family believed it showed their son Louis, in his twenties. The billboard stood by the highway for forty years. No explanation was ever confirmed.

caption:

No remains were found in the ashes; a coroner issued death certificates without them. The family put up a billboard by the highway, offered a reward, and kept it up for almost forty years. title: The Enigma Variations
subtitle: Elgar's hidden theme · London, 1899
vo: England, eighteen ninety-seven. Dora Penny received a cipher from Edward Elgar. Two years later, she became a piece of his music. London, June eighteen ninety-nine. The first performance of his Enigma Variations. Variation ten, called Dorabella, is a portrait of her. In the programme, Elgar said that through the whole set, another, larger theme goes, but is not played. He told her he thought she, of all people, would guess it. She never did. Elgar died in nineteen thirty-four without naming it. Dozens of answers have been proposed. None has ever been generally accepted.
